segments.text: What's up guys, welcome back to CrimeTimeSnacks.
Here is the strangest detail in the case file, stated plainly.
For decades, California police hunted three distinct monsters: the Visalia Ransacker, the East Area Rapist, and the Original Night Stalker.
They turned out to be one single man, and while he was committing his earliest attacks, he was wearing a police badge.
His name is Joseph James DeAngelo Jr. Between 1974 and 1986, he terrorized California, committing thirteen murders, more than fifty rapes, and well over one hundred burglaries.
Law enforcement agencies were completely siloed at the time, unable to easily share information across the county lines he crossed.
It took decades of dead ends before investigators realized the predator attacking suburban homes in Northern California was the exact same person murdering couples in Southern California.

The offender moved from breaking into houses in Visalia to assaulting victims in East Sacramento, Modesto, Stockton, and Contra Costa County, before escalating to murders in Santa Barbara, Ventura, and Orange counties.
He pried open doors and windows while victims slept, took personal souvenirs like coins and identification, and even taunted victims and police over the telephone.
The turning point came in 2001 when DNA testing finally linked the East Area Rapist to the Original Night Stalker crimes.
In 2013, author Michelle McNamara coined the name Golden State Killer to unite those scattered monikers under one roof.
Then in 2018, investigators uploaded a profile built from a preserved Ventura County rape kit to the open-source site GEDmatch, narrowing almost a million profiles down to a single family tree.
After watching his movements, authorities gathered DNA from the door handle of his car and a discarded tissue to confirm the match.
He was arrested outside his home at age seventy-two.
In 2020, DeAngelo pleaded guilty to thirteen counts of murder and multiple kidnappings to avoid the death penalty, ultimately receiving multiple life sentences without parole.
What the evidence actually shows is that this entire wave of violence started years earlier, in a quiet farming town in the Central Valley.
That is where we pick up the timeline.
The case file takes us to Visalia, halfway between Sacramento and Los Angeles.
Between April 1974 and December 1975, this farming community became the target of over one hundred burglaries.
The prowler, dubbed the Visalia Ransacker, bypassed major valuables in plain sight.
Instead, he rifled through personal belongings, scattered women's undergarments around rooms, and pocketed coins and low-value souvenirs.
At the very same time, Joseph DeAngelo was wearing a badge.
From 1973 to 1976, he worked as a police officer in nearby Exeter.
Law enforcement back then lacked cell phones, surveillance cameras, and shared computer databases.
In an era where agencies were heavily siloed, an offender with badge access and forensic awareness could operate across town lines with complete impunity.
The ransacking quickly turned deadly.
On September 11, 1975, an intruder broke into the Visalia home of professor Claude Snelling in an attempt to kidnap Snelling's daughter.
When the father intervened, the intruder shot him twice, kicked the daughter three times in the face, and fled into the night.
Snelling died from his wounds, marking the ransacker's first known homicide.
Three months later, in December 1975, another attempted break-in and shooting occurred in Visalia.
The ransacker slipped away from police once again, and just like that, the break-ins in town abruptly stopped.
What nobody realized then was that the prowler had simply packed up and moved his hunting grounds north.
By the summer of 1976, burglaries and rapes began terrorizing the eastern district of Sacramento County.
Prowling suburban single-story homes near open fields, an assailant known as the East Area Rapist began forcing open doors and windows.
The ransacker had evolved into something far more dangerous, bringing a brand new wave of fear to Northern California.
The case file shows that this was not random violence.
Joseph DeAngelo conducted extensive surveillance on his victims, memorizing their daily routines.
He would break into their houses beforehand to unlock windows, unload any firearms he found, and leave ligatures made of shoelaces or cords from the house lying ready for when he came back.
He telephoned some of them too, sometimes for months, learning when they were home and when they were alone.
At first, he targeted single women or mothers with young children, but soon he began targeting couples.
Victims would wake up to the blinding glare of a flashlight and a masked gunman standing right over their beds.
He tied up the man, often stacking dishes on his back with a direct threat: if those plates fell, he would kill them both.
Then he would assault the woman repeatedly, sometimes raiding the refrigerator for beer and food in between attacks before vanishing back into the dark.
The FBI noted that he routinely took cash, coins, jewelry, and identification from the residences he hit.
On the rare occasion someone spotted him, he escaped on a bicycle or scaled suburban fences, easily evading capture.
Between the lack of home surveillance, no cell phones, and the complete absence of DNA technology at the time, law enforcement was operating in the dark.
Agencies remained siloed, unable to track his movements across jurisdictional lines as his attacks continued across the East Bay.
Then came the night of February 1978 in the Sacramento area.
Brian and Katie Maggiore were simply out walking their dog through the neighborhood when they crossed paths with the prowler.
Prosecutors later revealed that DeAngelo shot Brian before chasing Katie down as she screamed for help, shooting her in the head.
The East Area Rapist had crossed the line into murder, and he was about to shift his hunting grounds entirely.
The murders of the Maggiores did not end the Northern California attacks.
They carried on around Sacramento and out into the East Bay through the middle of 1979.
Then, shortly after a rape that summer, the attacks shifted hundreds of miles south along the California coast, striking first in Santa Barbara County that October.
Between 1979 and 1986, a lethal new spree took hold in Southern California, eventually claiming at least ten lives.
Because the location changed and the primary outcome was now murder rather than sexual assault, investigators treated this as an entirely separate predator.
The press dubbed this new menace the Original Night Stalker.
That moniker was created to distinguish him from Richard Ramirez, the Night Stalker who terrorized the Los Angeles area during that same era.
In Ventura, the killer was also briefly known as the Diamond Knot Killer after victims Charlene and Lyman Smith were found bound with an unusual decorative nautical knot.
Across many of these Southern California scenes, ligatures were recovered, and victims were assaulted before being beaten to death or shot.
Back then, nobody put the pieces together.
Law enforcement agencies across different counties didn't communicate effectively, and the sheer geography of the crimes suggested independent offenders at work.
Without centralized tracking or DNA analysis to connect physical evidence across hundreds of miles, detectives found themselves running down false leads and hitting dead ends.
The killer effectively vanished into the suburban landscape between attacks, leaving behind taunting phone calls that continued to haunt past victims as late as 2001.
The case did not sit entirely still.
In 2001, DNA testing proved the East Area Rapist and the Original Night Stalker were the same man, and the two files became one under the acronym EARONS.
Then it went quiet again.

That changed when true crime writer Michelle McNamara began digging into the evidence, coining the name the Golden State Killer in 2013 to connect the Visalia Ransacker, the East Area Rapist, and the Original Night Stalker into one unified narrative.
By 2016, authorities launched a formal reinvestigation centered on modern forensic capabilities.
The physical evidence had survived decades in storage, and science was finally catching up to the man who left it behind.
Here is where the investigation turned into something unprecedented.
The national database, CODIS, uses about twenty STR markers to match identical profiles.
But solving this case required Investigative Genetic Genealogy, which uses single nucleotide polymorphisms, or SNPs.
That meant investigators needed hundreds of thousands of genetic markers, and their standard STR profiles could not translate over to genealogy systems.
STR and SNP profiles are completely incompatible, so detectives could not just port the old forensic files over into commercial databases.
To get the data, detectives had to pull physical evidence from cold storage.
They turned to a duplicate rape kit from 1980 that had been meticulously prepared, frozen, and preserved by a forward-thinking pathologist.
That preserved sample yielded the pristine, high-quality DNA required to build a completely new SNP profile.
In 2018, investigators uploaded that genetic data to the public sharing website GEDmatch, where users freely share profiles originally processed by commercial testing services.
The search did not return the killer directly.
Instead, it surfaced distant third and fourth cousins.
For four months, genealogists built out massive family trees, tracing separate ancestral lines backwards to find where they crossed.

By combining that genetic roadmap with traditional detective work, such as approximate age and geographic proximity, authorities narrowed almost a million profiles down to one family, and then to one man: former police officer Joseph James DeAngelo.
On April 19, 2018, police formally identified DeAngelo as their suspect and placed him under direct surveillance.
Investigators followed him, quietly collecting discarded items, including a swab from his car door handle and a used tissue he threw away.
The crime lab ran a standard STR test on that discarded sample.
It produced a flawless, direct match to the crime scene profile that had been waiting in CODIS for decades.
On April 24, 2018, authorities officially arrested and charged Joseph James DeAngelo.
After more than forty years of dead ends and terror across California, the predator who had stalked suburbs under multiple names was finally in handcuffs.

DeAngelo himself had never submitted his DNA.
He was exposed entirely because distant relatives did.
Privacy advocates raised sharp alarms about government overreach, arguing that trawling through public genetic databases amounts to a breach of basic privacy.
The reach of that science is immense.
